bai.moTa: Free fall cancels gravity, and therefore light must bend
bai.yChinh: In 1907 Einstein had a sudden realization: **a person in free fall does not feel their own weight**. It follows that inside a sufficiently small closed chamber, no experiment can distinguish standing at rest on the ground from sitting in an accelerating rocket, and free fall is indistinguishable from drifting through empty space. First consequence: light must bend in a gravitational field. Limitation: the chamber must be small; otherwise tidal forces appear.
bai.giaiThich:
- A chamber at rest on the ground and a chamber in a rocket accelerating at 9.8 m/s² give the same result in every local experiment: balls fall the same way, and scales read the same.
- Viewed from outside the rocket, a released ball stays put; it is the floor that rushes up to meet it. That is why all objects “fall” the same way, heavy or light. Experiments confirm the equality of inertial mass and gravitational mass to about $10^{-15}$.
- Free fall is the natural state of motion: a scale reads 0, and a falling chamber forms a local inertial frame. What we call weight is the ground pushing us up.
- A light beam crossing the rocket chamber curves downward relative to an observer inside; therefore light must also bend in a gravitational field.
- This holds only **locally**: in a wide chamber, two marbles falling side by side drift slightly closer together. That tidal force cannot be transformed away, and it is spacetime curvature itself (Lesson 12).
bai.conSo.1: **About 10⁻¹⁵**: the MICROSCOPE satellite (final results, 2022) showed that titanium and platinum test masses fall alike to this precision.
bai.conSo.2: **1971**: on the Moon, astronaut David Scott dropped a hammer and a feather at the same moment. They hit the ground together.
bai.conSo.3: **4.9 × 10⁻¹⁶ m**: the actual downward deflection of a light ray crossing a 3 m wide room on Earth.
bai.conSo.4: **8.7 m/s²**: gravitational acceleration at an altitude of 400 km, where astronauts are “weightless.”
bai.conSo.5: **0.73 micrometers**: how much two marbles 3 m apart move closer together because of tidal forces while falling 1.55 m.
bai.hieuDung: **The equivalence principle holds only in a small region.** In a very wide chamber on the ground, two balls dropped far apart fall along slightly converging paths because both point toward Earth’s center; in a rocket they fall along parallel lines. That convergence (a tidal force) cannot be eliminated by switching to a freely falling chamber. That is “real” gravity, and in general relativity it is precisely the *curvature of spacetime*.
bai.nguon: Einstein 1907 and 1911; Touboul et al. 2022 (MICROSCOPE, final results); NASA, Apollo 15 (1971). Accelerations, light deflection, and tidal effects are recalculated from CODATA 2018 constants and Earth’s GM (IAU); see kiem-tra/kiem-phan-3-cu.mjs.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.1: State the equivalence principle and explain what the word “locally” means in it.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.2: Explain why all objects “fall” alike in an accelerating rocket, and connect this to the equality of inertial and gravitational mass.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.3: Deduce from the closed-chamber argument that light must bend in a gravitational field, and calculate a light beam’s deflection across a room.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.4: Recognize tidal forces as the one aspect of gravity that free fall cannot cancel, and explain why they point to spacetime curvature.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.1.ten: The happiest thought: a falling person feels no weight
bai.baiGiang.buoc.1.noiDung:
You are looking at two closed chambers. The left chamber’s cable has snapped, and it is plunging toward Earth. The right chamber is the cabin of a spacecraft with its engine off, drifting through deep space far from any planet. In both, the person on the scale sees it read **0 kg**, the ball floats beside their hand, and the horizontal light beam travels straight to the target ring.

This was the insight that struck Einstein in 1907 while he was working at the Patent Office in Bern: someone falling freely from a roof **would not feel their own weight**. Everything around them falls the same way, so relative to them it remains at rest. He later called this the happiest thought of his life.

Here is the key question: if you were shut inside such a windowless chamber, could you tell whether you were falling toward Earth or drifting through empty space? Drop a ball, shine a lamp, step on a scale: both chambers give the exact same result.

> [Thử ngay] Drag the ball (the red dot) to the middle of a chamber and let go: it stays right there. Toss it gently and it drifts in a straight line at constant speed until it bounces off a wall. Then step outside to see what the two chambers are really doing.
> [[View from outside|ngoai]] [[Back inside the chamber|trong]]

> [Lưu ý] Every motion on screen is slowed down so the eye can follow it; light in particular is slowed by about a hundred million times.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.1.thuThach.de: Drag the ball in either chamber out toward the middle, more than 1 m above the floor, and release it gently enough that it **floats motionless** for 2 seconds.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.1.thuThach.goiY: Move slowly and pause briefly before letting go. If the ball drifts away, your hand was still moving at release: in a freely falling chamber, the ball keeps whatever velocity you give it.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.2.ten: Two chambers with weight: the ground and a rocket
bai.baiGiang.buoc.2.noiDung:
Now the left chamber sits at rest on the ground. The right chamber rides inside a rocket **accelerating uniformly at 9.8 m/s²** through empty space. The arrow beside each chamber shows what is going on: on the left, gravity pulls downward; on the right, an engine pushes upward.

Observers inside see the exact same thing in both places:

- the scale reads **70 kg**;
- a released ball falls to the floor with the same acceleration of 9.8 m/s²;
- a horizontal light beam hits the opposite wall at the same spot.

> [Định nghĩa] **{{Nguyên lý tương đương|Equivalence principle}}** (Einstein’s form): in a sufficiently small chamber over a sufficiently short time, no experiment can distinguish a chamber at rest in a gravitational field $g$ from a chamber accelerating uniformly at $a = g$ in a region free of gravity.

The phrase “no experiment” is sweeping: it covers not only mechanics, but also optics, electromagnetism, and atomic clocks. The phrase “sufficiently small” matters too; step 7 shows why.

> [Thử ngay] Drag the ball near the ceiling and release it in either chamber: it falls identically in both. Drag the **throttle** on the side of the rocket: stronger thrust makes the scale read above 70 kg and makes the ball fall faster, just like standing on a planet with stronger gravity. Drop a light object alongside the heavy ball: in both chambers they hit the floor together.
> [[Drop an extra light object|haiVat]] [[Single ball only|motVat]]

> [Lưu ý] About the sound: the low rumble is the engine noise transmitted to the passenger through the hull (empty space has no air to carry sound); it grows louder and harsher as you push up the throttle. The thud is the ball hitting the floor: the harder the impact, the louder the sound.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.3.ten: Seen from outside: the floor rushes up to meet the ball
bai.baiGiang.buoc.3.noiDung:
Now we stand outside beside two white reference rulers. Both rulers are at rest, so watching their tick marks tells you which chamber is moving.

- On the ground: the chamber sits still and the ball falls to the floor. Newton says: gravity pulls it down.
- In the rocket: the instant the ball leaves the hand, **no force acts on it**. It stays right where it was released. Meanwhile the engine keeps pushing the chamber upward faster and faster, and the floor rushes up to meet the ball.

The consequence is profound: in the rocket, “falling” has nothing to do with the ball itself. Iron or wood, heavy or light, every released object stays put and the floor catches up with all of them at the same instant. **In a rocket, it is automatic that all objects fall alike.** If a chamber on the ground is indistinguishable from the rocket, then on Earth too all objects must fall alike. That is just what Galileo found.

[[Drop an extra light object|haiVat]] [[Back inside the chamber|trong]]

> [Lưu ý] In the outside view, the scene replays a single drop and rewinds smoothly to the start so the rocket does not fly out of frame. Earth is drawn about a million times smaller than true scale.

+++ Go deeper: plotting the ball and the floor on a spacetime diagram
Put the time axis vertical and the height axis horizontal, as in Part 2. In the frame outside the rocket:

- After release, the ball stays at constant height $y = h$: its world line is a **vertical straight line**. With no force acting, its world line is straight.
- The floor has height $y = \tfrac12 a t^2$ (while its speed remains small compared with light): the floor’s world line is **curved**.

The two lines meet at the event “ball hits floor,” where $\tfrac12 a t^2 = h$, so $t = \sqrt{2h/a}$. For $h = 1{,}55$ m and $a = 9{,}8$ m/s², $t \approx 0{,}56$ seconds. The ball’s mass never enters: any object released from the same height meets the floor at the same time.

Strictly speaking, the floor’s world line is a branch of a hyperbola; the parabola $\tfrac12 at^2$ is its low-speed approximation. Lesson 8 draws this diagram in detail and uses it to show that a clock on the rocket’s ceiling runs faster than a clock on its floor.
+++
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.noiDung:
The two objects in each chamber (the heavy red ball and the light white marble) hit the floor together. In Newton’s theory, that is a suspicious coincidence, because mass plays **two distinct roles**:

- {{khối lượng quán tính|inertial mass}} $m_{\text{qt}}$: how reluctant an object is to accelerate when pushed, in $F = m_{\text{qt}}\,a$;
- {{khối lượng hấp dẫn|gravitational mass}} $m_{\text{hd}}$: how strongly Earth pulls on it, in $F = m_{\text{hd}}\,g$.

Combining the two gives $a = \dfrac{m_{\text{hd}}}{m_{\text{qt}}}\,g$. All objects fall alike only if the ratio $m_{\text{hd}}/m_{\text{qt}}$ is the same for every body and every material. Newton’s theory does not require this; it has to be tested by experiment.

> [Lịch sử] Galileo (early 17th century) used inclined planes and pendulums. Newton compared pendulums made of different materials. In the early 20th century, Loránd Eötvös used a torsion balance to push the precision to one part in a hundred million and then one part in a billion ($10^{-8}$ to $10^{-9}$). In 1971, Apollo 15 astronaut David Scott dropped a hammer and a feather on the airless Moon: they hit the ground together. The French satellite MICROSCOPE (launched in 2016, final results published in 2022) compared titanium and platinum test masses orbiting Earth: they fell alike to about $10^{-15}$.

Einstein read the equality the other way around: the two masses match not by luck, but because **falling is not a property of the object**. Falling is a property of space and time around the object, just as “falling” in the rocket is really the motion of the floor.

[[Drop two objects in the rocket, outside view|ngoai]] [[View inside the chamber|trong]]

+++ Go deeper: how precisely “alike” is measured
Experiments quantify any difference with the {{tham số Eötvös|Eötvös parameter}}: release two objects made of different materials, measure their accelerations $a_1$ and $a_2$, and form

$$ \eta = \frac{2\,|a_1 - a_2|}{a_1 + a_2}. $$

A bound of $\eta = 10^{-15}$ means that if two objects fell side by side for a thousand kilometers, they would separate by less than one quadrillionth of that distance, about one nanometer. MICROSCOPE did not drop objects from a height: two nested test masses sat inside a satellite orbiting Earth—and thus in continuous free fall—while instruments measured whether any force was needed to keep them in place relative to each other.
+++
bai.baiGiang.buoc.5.noiDung:
Return to the two weightless chambers from step 1, this time viewed from outside. The left chamber plunges toward the ground; the person, the scale, and the ball plunge with it at the exact same acceleration. Because the scale falls right along with the person’s feet, nothing presses down on it: **the scale reads 0**.

What, then, is the sensation we call “weight”? It is **the ground pushing us upward**, preventing us from following a path of {{rơi tự do|free fall}}. Standing on a scale at home, we are the ones being pushed, just like the passenger standing on the rocket’s floor.

Einstein turned Newton’s picture upside down:

- A freely falling chamber (if small enough) is a {{khung quán tính cục bộ|local inertial frame}}: inside it, free objects stay at rest or move in a straight line at constant speed, and all the laws of special relativity (Part 2) hold unchanged.
- Someone standing at rest on Earth’s surface is **not** in an inertial frame. They are accelerating upward at 9.8 m/s² relative to the local inertial frame right where they stand.

> [Hiểu sai thường gặp] “Astronauts float on the space station because there is no gravity up there.” Not so. At an altitude of about 400 km, gravitational acceleration is still roughly 8.7 m/s², nearly 90% of its value on the ground. Astronauts float because both they and the station are in **free fall** around Earth: falling continuously while moving sideways fast enough never to hit the ground.

> [Thử ngay] Push up the throttle on the side of the rocket: the floor begins to push on the passenger, their feet settle onto the scale, and the reading climbs above 0. That upward push is precisely what a scale measures.
> [[View from outside|ngoai]] [[Back inside the chamber|trong]]
bai.baiGiang.buoc.5.thuThach.de: The rocket on the right has its engine off, so its passenger is weightless. Adjust the **throttle** until the scale beneath their feet reads **70 kg** again, just like at home (within 3 kg).
bai.baiGiang.buoc.5.thuThach.goiY: The scale reads 70 kg times a/g. The yellow “1 g” mark on the throttle corresponds to a = 9.8 m/s². With nothing pushing the passenger upward, there is no weight.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.6.noiDung:
Watch the blue light beam in the two chambers with weight. The circle on the far wall marks where the beam would land if it traveled straight across (the dashed line). Instead, it hits the wall **lower down**: to an observer inside the chamber, the light’s path curves downward.

In the rocket, the reason is clear. Click “View from outside”: the light ray travels in a straight line, but while it crosses the cabin the whole chamber has shot upward, so the beam meets the far wall below the target ring.

By the equivalence principle, a chamber on the ground is no different from the rocket chamber. Therefore **a light beam on Earth must also curve downward**: gravity bends light. Einstein deduced this by reasoning alone, before having any equations of general relativity.

> [Con số] Light takes 10 nanoseconds to cross a 3 m wide room. In that time it drops by $\tfrac12 g t^2 \approx 4{,}9 \times 10^{-16}$ m, less than the size of a proton. On screen, light is slowed down by about a hundred million times so you can see the curve.

> [Thử ngay] Move the rocket’s throttle: stronger thrust bends the beam further; cut the engine and the beam goes straight.
> [[View from outside|ngoai]] [[View inside the chamber|trong]] [[Freely falling chamber, seen from the ground|roiNgoai]]

+++ Go deeper: from the closed chamber to starlight grazing the Sun
Let the chamber’s width be $L$. Crossing it takes $t = L/c$. In the chamber’s frame (accelerating at $g$), every free object has a downward acceleration $g$, light included, so the beam drops by

$$ \Delta y = \tfrac12 g \left(\frac{L}{c}\right)^2. $$

For $L = 3$ m and $g = 9{,}8$ m/s²: $t = 1{,}0 \times 10^{-8}$ s and $\Delta y \approx 4{,}9 \times 10^{-16}$ m.

Watching a freely falling chamber from the ground gives the same answer: inside the falling chamber the light ray goes straight; since the chamber is falling, relative to the ground the ray must curve downward along with it.

In 1911 Einstein used this very argument to estimate the deflection of starlight grazing the Sun’s limb, obtaining about 0.83 arcseconds (0.87 with modern values). In 1915, completed general relativity gave **twice** as much, about 1.75 arcseconds. The extra half comes from the curvature of space itself around the Sun, something a single small chamber cannot capture. Lesson 11 builds that spatial curvature; Lesson 14 tells the story of its measurement in 1919.
+++
bai.baiGiang.buoc.6.thuThach.de: Adjust the **throttle** so the light beam in the rocket hits the wall **half as far** below the target ring as the beam in the chamber on Earth.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.6.thuThach.goiY: The deflection $\Delta y = \tfrac12 a (L/c)^2$ is directly proportional to the acceleration $a$. The data panel at the bottom left shows the deflection in both chambers.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.7.noiDung:
Each chamber now holds four pink marbles released together: two side by side horizontally, and two one above the other. In the rocket chamber (right), they remain motionless relative to one another forever. In the chamber falling toward Earth (left):

- the two horizontal marbles **drift closer together**, because each falls straight toward Earth’s center along converging lines;
- the two vertical marbles **drift farther apart**, because the lower marble is slightly closer to Earth and feels a slightly stronger pull.

This is a {{lực thủy triều|tidal force}}. No choice of chamber can cancel it: a falling chamber cancels only the shared acceleration, not the **difference** between two places. Thus a wide enough chamber, observed long enough, can tell Earth apart from a rocket. The equivalence principle holds only **locally**.

> [Lưu ý] Tidal effects on screen are magnified millions of times. In reality, two marbles 3 m apart falling 1.55 m in a room move closer by only about 0.73 micrometers. Placed 1 km apart and dropped 500 m, they move closer by about 7.8 cm.

What remains after switching to free fall is “real” gravity. In general relativity, it is **spacetime curvature**: world lines that start out parallel draw closer together. Lesson 12 picks up the story from here.

> [Thử ngay] [[Hide test marbles|khongTrieu]] [[Show test marbles|trieu]] [[View from outside|ngoai]] [[View inside the chamber|trong]]

+++ Go deeper: calculating tidal acceleration
Place two marbles a horizontal distance $d$ apart at distance $R$ from Earth’s center. Each is pulled toward the center with acceleration $g$. The two pull directions converge by an angle $d/R$, giving a relative horizontal acceleration toward each other of

$$ \Delta a_{\text{ngang}} \approx g\,\frac{d}{R}. $$

With $d = 3$ m and $R = 6\,371$ km, $\Delta a \approx 4{,}6 \times 10^{-6}$ m/s². Over a fall of height $h$ (taking time $t$, with $h = \tfrac12 g t^2$), the marbles approach by $\tfrac12 \Delta a\, t^2 = d\,h/R$. Substituting $d = 3$ m and $h = 1{,}55$ m gives about $7{,}3 \times 10^{-7}$ m.

Vertically, gravitational acceleration $g = GM/r^2$ varies with altitude; differentiating gives $\Delta a_{\text{dọc}} \approx 2g\,d/R$, pulling the two marbles apart. Tides stretch vertically and squeeze horizontally—the same reason ocean water bulges on both sides of Earth under the Moon’s pull.
+++
bai.baiGiang.buoc.8.ten: From a thought to a theory
bai.baiGiang.buoc.8.noiDung:
Let us gather what a single closed chamber has taught us:

1. **All objects fall alike.** Falling is therefore a property of the space and time an object moves through, not of the object itself.
2. **Free fall is natural motion**, free of any force. Standing at rest on the ground is what requires an upward push.
3. **Light bends** in a gravitational field.
4. Applying the same argument to clocks: in an accelerating rocket, a clock on the ceiling runs faster than a clock on the floor; therefore on Earth, **a higher clock runs faster** than a lower clock. Lesson 8 proves this, and Lesson 9 measures it.
5. What cannot be canceled is the **tidal force**—that is, curvature.

> [Lịch sử] Getting from his 1907 insight to completed general relativity took Einstein eight years. The hardest part was learning unfamiliar mathematics: the geometry of curved spaces. He published the complete field equations in November 1915.

> [Tóm lại] Gravity is not a force in the ordinary sense. At any single point, you can cancel it by falling freely. What cannot be canceled is how local freely falling frames at nearby points fit together—and that is the geometry of spacetime.

[[Revisit the freely falling chamber|roi]] [[Revisit the accelerating rocket|nang]]
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.1.y: All objects fall alike if and only if the ratio $m_{\text{hd}}/m_{\text{qt}}$ is the same for every object.
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.2.y: Fractional difference in free-fall acceleration between two materials. MICROSCOPE (2022): about $10^{-15}$.
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.3.ten: Light deflection across a chamber of width L
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.3.y: For $L = 3$ m on Earth’s surface: $4{,}9 \times 10^{-16}$ m.
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.4.ten: Tidal acceleration (two objects separated by d)
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.4.y: $R$ is the distance to the center of attraction. Objects move closer horizontally and farther apart vertically.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.hoi: You wake up inside a windowless closed chamber. The scale under your feet reads 70 kg just like at home, and a dropped ball falls to the floor. What can you conclude for sure?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.chon.2: You are inside an accelerating rocket
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.chon.3: You could be either on Earth’s surface or in a rocket accelerating at 9.8 m/s²; local experiments cannot tell the difference
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.giai: That is the core of the equivalence principle. To tell the two apart, you would need either a very wide chamber (to detect tidal forces) or a look outside.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.hoi: On the Moon, a hammer and a feather dropped together hit the ground at the same moment. Why?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.chon.1: Because the Moon has no gravity
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.chon.2: Because each object’s gravitational mass is strictly proportional to its inertial mass, giving both the same free-fall acceleration
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.chon.3: Because the heavier hammer actually falls faster, and the measurement was simply too crude to tell
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.chon.4: Because the two objects have the same mass
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.giai: $a = (m_{\text{hd}}/m_{\text{qt}})\,g$. Gravity pulls harder on the hammer, but the hammer is proportionally harder to accelerate. On Earth a feather falls more slowly only because of air resistance; the Moon has no air.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.hoi: Astronauts aboard a space station in low Earth orbit (altitude about 400 km) float inside the cabin. Which statement is correct?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.chon.1: There is no gravity left at that altitude
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.chon.2: Gravity there is still nearly 90% as strong as on the ground, but the station and crew are in free fall together
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.chon.3: Thrust from the station’s engines balances gravity
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.chon.4: The station’s hull shields the interior from gravity
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.giai: At 400 km, $g$ is about 8.7 m/s². Weightlessness is a sign of free fall, not of “running out of gravity.” Saying that “centrifugal force balances gravity” merely describes the same motion in a frame rotating with the station.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.hoi: In an accelerating rocket, a horizontal light beam hits the far wall slightly lower down. Combined with the equivalence principle, what does this imply?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.chon.1: Light has mass and is therefore pulled downward
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.chon.2: Light must bend in a gravitational field
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.chon.3: The rocket slows the light down
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.chon.4: Nothing, because the effect occurs only inside rockets
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.giai: A chamber on Earth’s surface is locally indistinguishable from the rocket chamber, so whatever light does in the rocket it must also do on Earth. The argument does not require light to have mass.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.hoi: Inside a wide chamber falling freely toward Earth, two marbles are released at rest side by side horizontally, 3 m apart. Over time they will:
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.chon.1: Stay at the exact same separation forever
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.chon.2: Drift slightly closer together, because both fall toward Earth’s center
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.chon.4: Fall to the floor of the chamber together
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.giai: This is a tidal effect—tiny (about 0.73 micrometers over a 1.55 m fall) yet real and impossible to transform away. Vertically the opposite happens: two marbles drift apart. Choosing “fall to the floor” forgets that the floor is falling right along with them.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.6.hoi: Why was the equality of inertial mass and gravitational mass the key that led Einstein to view gravity as geometry?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.6.dap: If every object, regardless of mass or composition, follows the exact same path when launched from the same place with the same initial velocity, then a falling object’s trajectory carries no information about the object itself. It depends only on location and time—that is, on spacetime. Free-fall trajectories can therefore be understood as a geometric property of spacetime (its “straightest” paths) rather than the effect of a force acting on individual bodies. Electric forces are different: different charged particles follow different paths.
bai.baiGiang.docThem.1: A. Einstein, *Relativity: The Special and the General Theory* (1916), Part II: the closed chamber, equality of inertial and gravitational mass, and bending of light, told in everyday language.
bai.baiGiang.docThem.2: J. B. Hartle, *Gravity: An Introduction to Einstein’s General Relativity* (2003), chapter 6: Eötvös experiments, the equivalence principle, and freely falling frames.
bai.baiGiang.docThem.3: R. P. Feynman, *The Feynman Lectures on Physics*, Vol. II, chapter 42 “Curved Space”: the section on the equivalence principle and the accelerating rocket.
bai.baiGiang.docThem.4: K. S. Thorne, *Black Holes and Time Warps* (1994): the story of Einstein’s journey from his 1907 insight to general relativity.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.1.nghia: The mass in $F = ma$, measuring how strongly an object resists acceleration.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.2.nghia: The mass that determines how strongly a gravitational field pulls on an object. Experiments show it is strictly proportional to inertial mass.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.3.nghia: A reference frame attached to a small freely falling chamber. Over a small region and a short time, it acts as a true inertial frame of special relativity.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.4.nghia: The fractional difference in free-fall acceleration between two objects of different composition, $\eta = 2|a_1 - a_2|/(a_1 + a_2)$.

canh.nhin-tu-ben-ngoai-tren-mat-dat-qua: Outside view. On the ground: the ball falls to the floor. In the rocket: the ball stays put while the floor rushes up to meet it; the light ray goes straight, but the wall has moved up so the beam lands lower down. Two different stories, yet an observer inside measures the exact same thing.
canh.nhin-tu-trong-buong-hai-buong-giong: Inside view. The two chambers look identical: balls fall the same way, both scales read 70 kg, and both light beams droop by the same amount (the blue ring on the wall marks the straight-line spot). Drag a ball up and let go to test.
canh.nhin-tu-mat-dat-buong-trai-dang-roi: Seen from the ground. The left chamber is falling, and the person and ball fall with it, so the ball stays beside their hand. Because the light beam travels straight relative to the falling chamber, relative to the ground it must curve downward: gravity bends light.
canh.nhin-tu-trong-buong-khong-trong-luo: Inside view. Weightlessness in both places: the ball floats, the scale reads 0, and the light beam goes straight across. Someone inside the falling chamber cannot tell whether they are plunging toward Earth or drifting in deep space. Drag a ball and release it: it stays right there.
canh.can-ga-dang-o-m-s-g-can: Throttle at {0} m/s² ({1} g): the rocket scale reads {2} kg; how fast the ball falls and how much the light beam bends scale in that exact proportion.
canh.dung-yen-tren-mat-dat-bong-roi-9: at rest on the ground: ball falls at 9.8 m/s²
canh.tang-toc-m-s-can-chi-kg: accelerating at {0} m/s²: scale reads {1} kg
